Foundations Course V2 — L3

Jobs to Be Done, Positioning and Market Segmentation

Audience Question: If you're targeting B2B, do all the things we talked about apply to them — the emotions, the emotional drivers? Does that exist in B2B as well?

Broadly speaking, yes. We can see it even in the previous example. FUD — Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt — was aimed at a person, not at a company. The same person who has to make the decisions. In the end, there's always a person, no matter if it's a twenty-billion-dollar company. In the end, you're talking to a person, and that person has emotions, has interests that aren't always aligned with those of the company. And many times in B2B there are a lot of people who need to stand by your side and say yes, and you always need to think about what each of their interests are. IBM took this to an art form. They even coined the expression Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt. They tell the person, with such a critical investment for the company: if this computer goes down, the entire company will come to a standstill. Can you take that kind of risk? With IBM you're not taking a risk — you've covered yourself, you've done what you need to do.

A reverse example that I always love: people who invent a mechanism or method that can streamline work. How do they streamline it? "You don't need ten people, because my device does the work of ten people." Now you go to the manager who manages those ten people and explain to him why your product is worth it, because he's not paying ten salaries but rather twenty thousand dollars a year. And you can't understand why he's explaining to you that you're wrong. You can't replace the people, because you don't need a manager for a twenty-thousand-dollar machine — you need to manage ten people.

I have a story about myself, even at ZoomInfo. We were looking for customers, and we gathered our information from newspapers and press releases. We said: there are great customers — the Development Office of every university in the United States. What does the Development Office do? They read the papers and say, "Wow, Yonatan Stern made an exit. He studied at the Technion, let's call him, explain to him that the exit happened because he studied at the Technion, so he should donate a fifty-thousand-dollar-a-year scholarship for outstanding students." That's how American culture works. We call them up and say: you don't need to read the newspapers, we have a machine that does it for you, identifies that the person is an alumnus. In this case it was the University of Pennsylvania. The salesperson came back afterward and told me: "You won't believe what I heard. I call this woman, explain everything to her, she's super excited, and we're practically best friends, and then she says: honestly, I don't need your product. I have ten people here who do this every day, and they do a great job." He came back to me stunned. I told him: why are you surprised? Her entire job is to manage those ten people. She's not responsible for the university's budget. You have to remember that — in the end, there are always people.

The last sentence here is the most important, and that's why I left it on the screen. In the end — at least in my view, and this is what I preach to the companies we work with — companies want the job to be done. That's what they want, and also the level of risk they take is much lower. Let's say you have an inventory optimization system. You give the customer two options. Option one: I'll give you the machine, teach you how to use it, and your people will do all the work. Option two: once a month we'll bring you an updated report on which inventory to decrease and which to increase, and we'll do all the work for you. How much will it cost? Two thousand dollars a month. And if after three months you're not happy, fire us.

The second decision is much easier for them for several reasons. First of all, companies are used to hiring consultants — you don't need special budgets, the whole process is familiar to them, not complicated, and you don't even need to define precisely what he'll do. A product, on the other hand, looks like a big commitment: you need to understand it, use it, what will it do, what will it cause. By the time you've finished selling it, you're old and gray. So many times, don't be shy: my product is brilliant, but you don't need it — I'll do the work for you, here's what I charge.

As someone told us yesterday: she has a brilliant product, tried to sell it for years, and has three paying customers — that's all she has after years of work. Now she started selling just the output. She sells one project at a price that's roughly seventy percent of the system's price, and they need about twenty projects a year, and they have no problem at all — they pay her enthusiastically. She says, "I'm completely stunned." Yes, because people don't want products, they don't want to learn anything. Do the work for me at a price cheaper than what it costs me, and everything's great. That's the most important lesson I can tell you here. And don't sell it to the woman who manages the ten people — go to the CEO. Ask him, "Are you happy with the efficiency in your company?" and he'll say, "Yeah, everything's fine." "Do you think there are things you could have saved on?" And then you start uncovering things. And it turns out it's not just ten people — two are on maternity leave, two are on reserve duty, and one is in jail because they discovered he was stealing credit cards. Happened to me. People — they're the best thing there is, completely unpredictable.

Market Segmentation. Let's look at another example: airlines, Airline Tickets, and we want to do this by context — Business Trips. The question: how do airlines know who's buying a ticket for business and who isn't? I'm not talking about business class, but a businessperson buying a regular ticket versus someone who wants to vacation in New York. How do you find out? By how far in advance they book the ticket, and by the days.

Businesspeople — for example me, when I used to fly Israel–Boston–Israel at a crazy pace — I had an almost permanent ticket on Saturday night. Why? I get on the plane Saturday night, arrive in Boston Sunday at six-thirty in the morning, and Monday I'm already at work, relaxed after a night's sleep. Thursday afternoon I get on the plane, and Friday at noon I'm home. Nobody noticed I was gone. Most businesspeople don't want to be away from home on the weekend, for obvious reasons. So on domestic flights within the United States, they get on the plane Sunday evening, arrive at night, go to the hotel, and Monday morning they show up refreshed. Thursday afternoon, everyone — like a plague — heads to the airport. Everyone flying between Sunday and Thursday is business. Everyone who gets on Friday and comes back Sunday night is not a businessperson.

Now, the same ticket on El Al that I used to take cost, say, two thousand dollars. If I had flown on a Tuesday it would have cost eight hundred dollars. Why? Because I need to get to the flight at that specific place and time, and besides, the one paying is the company. So let the company suffer — why should my wife or kids suffer? Who pays the money is a very critical thing. If it comes out of your pocket, I'm willing to fly on a different day. If it's the company — I need to be home.

Now you need to turn this into something emotional, and here it starts getting more interesting. They invented business class. On domestic flights within the United States it's virtually meaningless, there's almost no difference, but they try to give it a difference. On international flights it's different: you get more service on the ground, you can go into the lounge, you get slightly bigger crackers, better seats. If I add up all the perks, they're worth about twelve and a half dollars, even though you paid twelve hundred. But there's an even better idea — the Miles Program. What do they do with the Miles? They create a dual effect. A, an Incentive for the ticket price to be as high as possible, because in business you get triple points. B, now you have loyalty to the airline — you want to fly exclusively with El Al to accumulate points, because if you spread it across five airlines you'll never collect enough. That's how they decoupled the company's interest from the loyalty of the person booking the ticket.

C and last, Social Symbol. "How do you fly to America? I only fly business, I don't mix with the masses. There's a limit — you expect me to sit next to someone with a baby? No." All of these things play a very significant role in Jobs to Be Done.

Let's take another interesting case. An entrepreneur came to us — let's call him Moishe — and he had an amazing idea. He built a thermos with a built-in water-heating mechanism powered by batteries. It works. He put it on Kickstarter at eighty-nine dollars per unit and sold thirteen hundred units pretty quickly. And now he came to consult on how to Scale Up.

[Clip from the Chemos marketing video]
The product — Chemos, "the king of all thermoses" — a self-heating thermos that reaches a full boil in three minutes, can do it five times before recharging, and keeps the water hot for four hours. Safe to use even with boiling water, light, simple. The video shows a range of uses: coffee in the woods, preparing baby food at sterilization temperature, a hot drink in traffic jams, tea in the desert, on top of a pyramid, and in the cold mountains.

First of all, let's go back to the homework. Here's a great example of how to sell a product that doesn't exist. This product doesn't exist — there's a nice video, but there's no product. They put the video on Kickstarter and that's how they raised the money, but the product was never manufactured. That's not the point here. The point is that when I talk to you about "sell first, test the market before" — here's a way. This entire video cost something in the range of ten thousand dollars. By the way, the guy doesn't even speak English, but he hired consultants and worked with them and produced this. Now he comes, and the question was how do we help him start doing marketing.

The first thing I told him: let's see who the competitors are. It turns out there's a competitor called Ember with a similar product. I said: we need to do jobs to be done, something that will differentiate their product from ours. This was about a year and a half ago. And we came up with an idea: let's go with mothers of babies. He already touched on this in the video too. It's fantastic, because there's a very precise definition: mothers outside the home need to prepare formula for their baby, and they need water that boils to a hundred degrees so it's sterilized, otherwise it's terrible. They worry that if there's no water something will happen, and it's also uncomfortable to go and ask someone for boiling water. We sat and celebrated the brilliant idea and said: let's build the campaign.

And then I went to look at Ember again, and look what I saw: two weeks after we discussed the idea — boom! Baby bottle system. The price went from a hundred forty-nine to four hundred dollars. And remember, as I said about the full product — there are also nipples, and it looks like a baby kit. Everything a young mother needs, and a price that's suitable for gifts. We were embarrassed, but that's how it is.

And then I went to check again what Ember is doing. I read the text: "Designed for home or office." Notice — home or office, not on the pyramids, not kids. "The Ember Mug2 does more than simply keep your coffee hot. Our smart mug allows you to set an exact drinking temperature." Notice — the Jobs to be done changed. What I'm trying to show is the gap between the product — a machine that heats itself — and the needs, what problem are you solving. Here's a company that's probably more successful than Chemos, and they too had to pivot. When you think about it logically, there are far more people sitting in an office who like their coffee at seventy-two degrees than mothers with babies or hikers on the Himalayas. Their understanding was that this is what people are willing to pay for, and that's the right positioning. The product is the same product. Remember that.

Question: How do you decide to look at the jobs to be done based on competitors and not on the market, and how do you determine that a competitor is more successful? I don't have magic solutions. The purpose of this lecture is only to explain that you need to look at what you're doing in a much deeper way and from different angles. I just want to show that even this specific competitor went through almost the entire journey we did: we said "let's try this for mothers" — boom, they did it, and then they pulled that product off their website. How do you know what the job to be done is? You do everything that can give you information. You look at what competitors are doing — they're spending a lot of money, and they're probably doing things that are succeeding in selling. And also — you just try to sell. He sold thirteen hundred units on Kickstarter, so there was demand, but at too low a price to build a good enough company.

Question about the patent: Yes, they have a patent. It's worth taking a two-minute detour on this topic. What is a patent? An American invention from the nineteenth century that allows you to protect intellectual property. The problem is how you define what's patentable. The definition says it has to be something that a person in the field doesn't consider trivial. Notice how poorly defined that is. Second definition: that you're the first to invent it, not the first to write it down — at least in my time. (From the audience: Today it's first to file, and that's worldwide.) I have, by the way, six patents to my name. What do I do with them? Hang them on the wall.

Going deeper: the patents we filed at ZoomInfo were on the technology, and there was a ton of innovative technology there. There's just one problem: if someone violates the patent and codes a similar idea, I don't know about it, because at most I see the output, and they could have arrived at it through ten different methods. The patent doesn't protect me in any way, other than personal satisfaction. When we debated whether to publish the technology or keep it a secret, the guy who developed some of the algorithms told me: "You want to protect your patent so nobody copies it? Publish it in a scientific journal, because there it's guaranteed nobody will read it." In short, all a patent allows you to do is sue whoever violates it, and they immediately file a countersuit saying the patent never belonged to you in the first place.

True story: at CardScan we had a scanner. Then USB was invented, and USB has a power line, so you can charge through it. One day I get a lawsuit saying I'm violating a patent from a scanner manufacturer who has a patent on a scanner that can be charged via USB. I told them: "Are you kidding me? That's part of the USB specification." They said, "We got a patent." The patent clerk was asleep at that moment, who knows. I said, "Fine, sue me, I'll give up the patent." So they said, "We have a better offer: I can manufacture your scanner at a lower price than my competitors." Well, that sounds interesting. In short, they became my supplier. So the patent worked — they called me, and they do excellent work.

Now, Chemos with Travelers to exotic countries — trips to places like India or Mozambique. The function here is that it can bring the temperature up to a hundred degrees, and nobody on a trip like that wants to be sick and have diarrhea in a hotel room instead of being out in the jungle. And it's also not pleasant to go around asking for boiled water everywhere. Why am I bringing all this up? To show the impact of this concept on the product. Look, the product here looks different — there are no nipples, but if you're traveling the world you need a carrier that looks nice, and a spare battery, because you're in the heart of the jungle and there's nowhere to plug in, and I'll also give you a charger. The exact same idea keeps coming back. It's the jobs to be done. If I'm selling to pregnant women, I sell things that are relevant to a baby. If you're traveling to the jungle, I sell things related to jungle travel.

Let's talk a bit about my experience. I told you about CardScan and the patents, but let me tell you about Jobs to be done at Rosh Thinking Systems. The company was founded in eighty-four and we raised around twelve million dollars. What was the product? AI from a long time ago — they called it Expert System back then. The idea was that we'd help service technicians for complex systems: Philips Medical, Siemens Medical, Xerox, Applied Materials, Lam Research — big companies in the field of complex chip manufacturing machines. We gave them an Expert System on a laptop, so the technician could figure out what was broken in the system. Today that's common, for example in vehicles, but I'm talking about forty years ago.

Before they invested money in us, they said "Show me there's even demand." We started going around the United States and a bit in Europe, talking to potential customers, and our job was to get them to agree to be our Beta site. There was a lot of interest, and they were willing to sign, and that's how we raised the money. I moved to Boston in eighty-nine. The company grew, but it wasn't profitable.

And then one day I went to one of our big customers and asked an annoying question. Alongside us there was another company that didn't develop Expert Systems and AI — all they developed was CRM for service organizations, where each technician manages their own service calls. We had reached four million dollars, they were in the twenty million range, and that really bothered me. I asked the customer, who had both our product and the CRM: "You told me this is a great product, so why are you spending more money with them than with me?" And he said to me: "You asked the wrong question." That message has stayed in my head to this day. I asked "What's the right question?" He said: "You should have asked me — if I have a hundred thousand dollars in my budget, would I buy Rosh's product or something else?"

He explained: "I have a hundred technicians driving around in cars between customers, and each one has spare parts in the trunk. I have over a hundred million dollars' worth of spare parts sitting in car trunks, and I have no idea where each part is. That's much more critical to me than an Expert System for repairs." At that moment I realized I had truly asked the wrong question. When you ask what the Jobs to be done are, that's the right question. You go to the customer and ask "What keeps you up at night? If you had a hundred dollars, what would you spend them on?" And it turns out it's not about you at all. Many times their solution is trivial — CRM is not the pinnacle of technology. Look at the situation from the customer's perspective.

We founded ZoomInfo in two thousand, and there I built Deep AI Technology — Expert Systems were no longer enough for me. It was about language understanding, extracting information from the internet. We're talking about the year two thousand, before all of today's AI. We crawled the internet, read newspapers and Press Releases, and extracted information from the text. We started in two thousand and two, became profitable pretty quickly, grew nicely, but our market was Recruiters and Head hunters. In that market we were very successful — the product cost a thousand dollars a month per seat and they paid, because I solved a problem for them. A client comes and says "I want to recruit a VP Sales for a software company in the fifty-million-dollar range in the Boston area." The Head hunter would scratch his head, and I came along and gave him a list of a hundred names with all the articles and Press Releases. I created a book for him that he takes to the client.

But here's the thing — it's a small market. How many Head hunters are there? But there's a huge market — salespeople, who also need names. So let's go after that market. And then we ran into a problem: our product solved one problem but not another. The Jobs to be done for HR and Recruiters was to prepare a basic list with a lot of data around it, that would look impressive, because I did extensive research work to get the job. After we went over the list with the client, they'd say "there are ten here that interest us," and we'd pick up the phone and call those ten people — not complicated, because when a Head hunter calls a VP Sales, he always answers.

Salespeople are a completely different story. Head hunters are looking for a needle in a haystack — one candidate the client will love. Salespeople want the entire haystack, because they make a hundred phone calls a day. They don't care who the person is, only that he's the VP Sales at a company over fifty million dollars. Give me the right phone number and email, I'll get straight to work. Wait, you don't have phone numbers? Then what are you worth? And there are no phone numbers on the internet — our system collected data but didn't have access to phones and emails. In short, our product for salespeople was worth zero. They cared about five things: Name, Title, Company, Email, Phone Number — and they need to be accurate, and there need to be lots of them. Notice — the Jobs to be done for Recruiters and for salespeople was completely different. We were in shock.

It took us two or three years to figure out what to do and build a new product that solves the problem. Why do I keep saying "profitable company"? Because you can make mistakes and not die. The company was profitable, the HR and Head Hunter people supported it well. We made a mistake, but we could set up a team to solve the problem. Today that's the basic model of all the companies competing with ZoomInfo: they all scrape LinkedIn or buy its data, they have a network of contributors who give access to their email box and from there they extract phone numbers, and then they add more things on top. Everyone does the same thing — Apollo, Lusha, People, and so on.

Question: How did you get from CardScan to ZoomInfo, where did the idea come from? They drove me crazy at the end of the nineties. CardScan was profitable and growing, and everyone was saying "Yonatan, what are you doing with the internet?" Because that was the peak of the internet bubble. I said "I'm selling CardScan on the internet," and they told me "You're kidding me, where's the Disruptive Technology?" It's not hard to understand: the internet has two strong legs. One — an amazing communications platform, every place is connected to every place. The second — all the information in the world is there. When I looked at the search engines of that time, I saw that the information you're looking for exists in many cases, but you can't get it. For example, if I want all the companies in Ra'anana — if someone bothered to make a list, I'll find it; if not, I won't get an answer. But every company in Ra'anana has a website. The answer exists, you just need to discover it and organize it in a database.

So the idea was to build technology that knows how to read the entire internet, extract information and put it in databases. And you didn't have to be a genius after CardScan to understand that the people who would pay for this are people who consume names and information about companies. So we focused on that area. But the real reason was intellectual curiosity: can I build this crazy thing, the one the board told me "absolutely no way are we going to let you do"? Twenty years later they were pretty happy about it.

Now let's do segmentation in a different way. I'm showing you a product called a watch. Its purpose is to show the time. And it doesn't matter if I have a Rolex, Apple, or Timex — the time is three seventeen. So why is there such variety? Rolex is a social status symbol. If I can spend fifty thousand dollars on a watch, I probably have fifty thousand dollars to waste (although that's not always true — when you don't have a penny and you want a loan from the bank, you rent a Mercedes and a driver, like in the movies). Swatch went in a different direction — a fashion product. You can change your watch twice a day to match your outfit, it's a fashion statement. Sure, it also shows the time, but that's almost irrelevant. Apple Watch — emotional. You want a gadget that does everything, you're the first one on the block who bought it, showing it to everyone, making sure the screen changes constantly so nobody misses it. And Timex — the watches I love: twenty dollars, they work, they show the time.

But a product requires packaging. How do you make a Rolex watch into a social status symbol? It didn't get there by accident — there are people who work hard to make sure of that. First, you make sure the price is ridiculous — forty to fifty thousand dollars. You can't have a status symbol that costs twenty-five dollars. And then you need to create scarcity, because scarcity drives up the price. There's a waiting list of about two years, carefully managed. And if I walk into a store and ask to buy a Rolex, they politely explain "Who do you think you are? Do you have proof that you've been chasing Rolex since you were seventeen?" You know Groucho Marx — he wouldn't join any club that would have him as a member, because that immediately lowers the standards. You have to prove yourself.

What are the side effects? There's a second hand market. I have a friend who orders two luxury watches every year. I ask him "What for?" and he says "Because a week later I sell them at a twenty percent profit." It's an investment asset with appreciating value, and also collector items similar to art. Patek Philippe tells you: you're not buying the product, you're not using it — you're holding it for your children, because it's an asset. They produce sixty-eight thousand watches a year, intentionally few, to create demand. Breitling — those are the ones you always see on small airplanes. Omega and Rolex produce a million a year. That's how you create a luxury product. Notice — that's the social parameter. Look how hard they work, and it's not about the time at all. Nobody cares about the time.

There's a problem — women aren't interested in watches. But there's something to do with women: handbags. This thing costs in the range of twenty to thirty thousand dollars, and it's not open to just anyone. You walk into an Hermès store, and you need to prove you spend several thousand dollars every year, that you're worthy of being spoken to. You register and buy every year, and then after a certain period they approach you politely: "Mrs. Stern, you meet the requirements. Would you like to sign up for our Birkin bag? The waiting time is about seventeen years, but you still look young." Notice — there's another dimension here: emotional. For men and women it's not the same thing. No man would buy a Birkin unless he's trying to court someone. Women buy bags, men buy watches.

Until now you've decided this is B2C. What does this have to do with the things that we, the geniuses of the generation with our disruptive technology, do? So IBM, as Thomas Watson said: "I think there is a world market for maybe five computers." That was in the late forties. In the seventies there was a lot of competition over the main frame, but they were at the top of the list from the sixties through the eighties. Let's do the four-dimension breakdown again. What's the function? Business administration — accounting, inventory. No disruptive technology, just databases for managing complex operations. What's the context? Big companies — banks, large corporations that already have operations requiring computing.

Emotional — that's the key point. IBM developed a well-known sales methodology. They're called Big Blue because their salespeople always wore a blue suit and blue tie — it was a uniform. They had a method called FUD — Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt. They'd talk to the CIO and say: "You need to buy a new main frame? Look, you can buy CDC, Burroughs, Cray — they're all good computers. But what happens if on Monday morning the computer goes down and the bank is closed? What will the CEO say? Why did you buy Burroughs? You saved me two million dollars and now I look like an idiot. You bought IBM — nobody will ask you why." It's CYA: "I bought the best computer, the fact that it's not perfect isn't my fault, so I won't lose my job." And still — don't buy, but your competitors already have computers, you should probably get one too.

And then in ninety-three IBM loses eight billion dollars — quite a lot of money. They bring in a new CEO, Lou Gerstner, who was the CEO of RJR Nabisco — a snacks and cigarettes company, the most basic consumer products — and before that CEO of American Express. It has nothing to do with technology. I was in the United States at that time and I remember it like yesterday: endless articles by analysts saying "The leading technology company brings in the CEO of RJR Nabisco, they've lost their minds." They interview the guy: "What are you going to do?" and he says "I'm going to visit customers, hear what they want." Everyone laughed at him — "What a stupid answer, you're the CEO of the leading technology company."

After a few months of going around without opening his mouth, he came back and said "I understand. We're going to turn IBM into Professional Managed Services for the same customers." Why? "Because when I went to the bank and asked what they need, they said: it's gotten complicated to manage a computer, you're being attacked from every direction. We need someone to be our IT, 24/7, to make everything work, to keep the bank protected. If you can't give me that, I'll go to McKinsey or EY." He discovered that all the customers don't want a computer — they want a solution. So he turned IBM into a Professional Services company. That's why you haven't heard much about them for a long time — they work with banks and large corporations and manage their computing centers. In 2023 they earned seven and a half billion dollars on sales of sixty-two billion. So Jobs to be done exists everywhere.

Why did IBM fall from its greatness? This is my personal opinion. There are two companies that had an astronomical decline, each in a different way: IBM and Xerox. IBM said "We're a big computer company, there are these little PC's, let's make a PC," but they treated it as a toy. They decided to publish how to build their PC — they called it PC Compatible — and gave it to anyone who wanted it. But you also needed an operating system, and then a kid came to them and said "I have an operating system." The kid's father was a well-known lawyer, and he said "Let's put in exclusivity." IBM said "Forget it, it's not relevant, we'll sign and be done." And so the PC, because now companies could manufacture a standard compatible PC with a uniform operating system, spread like wildfire. Gradually this tool became more powerful, sat on Local Area Networks that were developed at Xerox, and started delivering a lot of what the mainframe did — at cheap prices. And since IBM published everything and didn't take control of the market, they lost.

The thing that amazed me: you'd think they only dealt with mainframes and not consumer products, but that's not true. They had a huge division for typewriters — the typewriters with the ball. They had a strong and impressive B2C, and somehow nobody talked to anybody, and they came out with the PC and shot themselves in the foot. Xerox did something similar: they developed a computer that invented windows, WYSIWYG, menus, the mouse, Local Area Network, Laser Printer — everything you see today in the modern computer was developed at Xerox PARC (Palo Alto Research Center). They called it the Star, and Xerox said "we're not interested" — why, I still don't understand to this day. Steve Jobs was interested, came out with the Lisa in 1985 and right after that with the Macintosh, the first computer that implemented the ideas developed at Xerox PARC. The rest is history.

Homework. Why am I giving you homework? Over twenty people submitted last time, and a few people said they suffered greatly but it helped them. So this time you'll suffer greatly too. The homework consists of two assignments. The first one is related to olive oil. Find at least four different jobs to be done where olive oil can serve — different contexts, different emotions. Pick two that are innovative and interesting to you and write some copy for ads. Think about how it affects the business model: where will you sell it, at what price, what packaging. I'm deliberately giving you the simplest product that exists — five thousand years on this planet. The Romans even bathed in olive oil. Put it in a new positioning. You're allowed to use the internet because it's fun — I just want you to see the enormous diversity and the effect it will have once you start thinking about who am I selling to, why will they buy.

The second project — the same thing for your own product. Define three different jobs to be done, do the analysis according to functional, contextual, emotional, and write copy for each positioning. Think about it from the user's perspective: if they're going to use my product for this purpose, what else do they need to be happy? We'll send it to you by email, and in a week and a half, on Monday, we'd be happy to receive the homework. Thank you very much — this time we stayed on schedule.

How do you make a Rolex watch into a social status symbol? הוא לא הגיע לשם במקרה — יש אנשים שעובדים קשה כדי לדאוג לזה. קודם כל, אתה דואג שהמחיר יהיה מגוחך — ארבעים-חמישים אלף דולר. לא יכול להיות status symbol שעולה עשרים וחמישה דולר. ואז אתה צריך לייצר מחסור, כי מחסור מעלה את המחיר. יש רשימת המתנה של בערך שנתיים, מנוהלת בקפדנות. ואם אני נכנס לחנות ומבקש לקנות רולקס, בעדינות מסבירים לי "מי אתה חושב שאתה? יש לך תעודה שאתה מגיל שבע עשרה רודף אחרי רולקס?" אתם מכירים את גראוצ'ו מרקס — הוא לא הולך לשום קלאב שמוכן לקבל אותו כחבר, כי זה מיד מוריד את הרמה. אתה צריך להוכיח את עצמך.

מה ה-side effects? יש second hand market. יש לי חבר שכל שנה מזמין שני שעוני יוקרה. שואל אותו "בשביל מה?" והוא אומר "כי שבוע אחרי זה אני מוכר אותם ברווח של עשרים אחוז". זה investment asset with appreciating value, וגם collector items similar to art. פאטק פיליפ אומרים לך: אתה לא קונה את המוצר, לא משתמש בו — אתה מחזיק אותו בשביל הילדים, כי זה asset. הם מייצרים שישים ושמונה אלף שעונים בשנה, בכוונה מעט, שיהיה ביקוש. ברייטלינג זה אלה שתמיד רואים על מטוסים קטנים. אומגה ורולקס עושים מיליון בשנה. ככה אתה מייצר מוצר יוקרה. שימו לב — זה הפרמטר של social. תראו כמה קשה הם עובדים, בכלל לא על השעה. השעה לא מעניינת אף אחד.

יש בעיה — נשים לא מתעניינות בשעונים. אבל יש מה לעשות עם נשים: תיקים. הדבר הזה עולה סדר גודל של עשרים-שלושים אלף דולר, ולא פתוח לכל אחת. את נכנסת לחנות הרמס, וצריכה להוכיח שאת קונה בכמה אלפי דולרים כל שנה, שאת שווה שידברו איתך. את נרשמת וקונה כל שנה, ואז אחרי זמן מסוים פונים אלייך בנימוס: "גברת שטרן, את עומדת בתנאים. את רוצה להירשם לתיק הברקין שלנו? זמן ההמתנה הוא בערך שבע עשרה שנה, אבל את עוד נראית צעירה". שימו לב — יש פה עוד חתך: emotional. אצל גברים ונשים זה לא אותו דבר. אף גבר לא יקנה ברקין אלא אם הוא רוצה לחזר אחרי מישהי. נשים יקנו תיק, גברים יקנו שעון.

עד עכשיו אתם החלטתם שזה ל-B2C. מה הקשר לדברים שאנחנו, גאוני הדור עם ה-disruptive technology שלנו, עושים? אז IBM, כמו שאמר תומאס ווטסון: "I think there is a world market for maybe five computers". זה היה בסוף שנות הארבעים. בשנות השבעים הייתה הרבה תחרות על ה-main frame, אבל הם היו ברשימה למעלה בין שנות השישים לשמונים. נעשה שוב את החלוקה לארבעת הממדים. מה הפונקציה? Business administration — accounting, מלאים. שום disruptive technology, פשוט מסדי נתונים לניהול פעילות מסובכת. מה הקונטקסט? Big companies — בנקים, חברות גדולות שכבר יש להן פעילות שמחייבת מחשוב.

Emotional — זו הנקודה המרכזית. IBM פיתחו שיטת מכירה ידועה. הם נקראים Big Blue כי אנשי המכירות תמיד לבשו חליפה כחולה ועניבה כחולה — זה היה מדים. הייתה להם שיטה בשם FUD — Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt. דיברו עם ה-CIO ואמרו: "אתה צריך לקנות main frame חדש? תראה, אתה יכול לקנות CDC, בורוז, קריי — כולם מחשבים טובים. אבל מה יקרה אם ביום שני בבוקר המחשב נופל והבנק סגור? מה יגיד המנכ"ל? למה קנית בורוז? חסכת לי שני מיליון דולר ועכשיו אני נראה כמו מטומטם. קנית IBM — אף אחד לא ישאל אותך למה". זה כסת"ח: "קניתי את המחשב הכי טוב, זה שהוא לא perfect זה לא אשמתי, אז לא אאבד את מקום עבודתי". ובכל זאת — אל תקנה, אבל המתחרים שלך כבר יש להם מחשבים, כדאי שגם אתה תקנה.

ואז בשנת תשעים ושלוש IBM מפסידה שמונה מיליארד דולר — די הרבה כסף. מביאים מנכ"ל חדש, לואו גרסטנר, שהיה המנכ"ל של RJR נביסקו — חברת חטיפים וסיגריות, מוצרי צריכה הכי בסיסיים — ולפני זה מנכ"ל של American Express. אין לזה שום קשר לטכנולוגיה. הייתי בארצות הברית באותה תקופה וזוכר את זה כמו היום: אינסוף מאמרים של אנליסטים שאומרים "החברה הכי מובילה בטכנולוגיה מביאה את המנכ"ל של RJR נביסקו, איבדו את הצפון". מראיינים את הבחור: "מה אתה הולך לעשות?" והוא אומר "אני הולך לבקר את הלקוחות, לשמוע מה הם רוצים". כולם צחקו עליו — "איזו תשובה מטומטמת, אתה המנכ"ל של חברת הטכנולוגיה המובילה".

אחרי כמה חודשים שהסתובב ולא פתח את הפה, הוא חזר ואמר "הבנתי. אנחנו הולכים להפוך את IBM ל-Professional Managed Services for the same customers". למה? "כי כשהלכתי לבנק ושאלתי מה הם צריכים, הם אמרו: נהיה מסובך לנהל מחשב, תוקפים אותך מכל פינה. אנחנו צריכים מישהו שיהיה ה-IT שלנו, 24/7, שהכל יעבוד, שהבנק יהיה מוגן. אם אתה לא יכול לתת לי את זה, אלך למקינזי או ל-EY". הוא גילה שכל הלקוחות לא רוצים מחשב — הם רוצים פתרון. אז הפך את IBM לחברת Professional Services. לכן לא שמעתם עליה הרבה זמן — היא עובדת עם הבנקים והחברות הגדולות ומנהלת להם את מרכזי המחשוב. ב-2023 הם הרוויחו שבעה וחצי מיליארד דולר על מכירות של שישים ושתיים מיליארד. אז Jobs to be done קיים בכל מקום.

למה IBM ירדה מגדולתה? זו דעתי האישית. יש שתי חברות שעשו שקיעה אסטרונומית, כל אחת בדרך אחרת: IBM וזירוקס. IBM אמרו "אנחנו חברת מחשבים גדולה, יש מין PC's כאלה, בואו נעשה PC", אבל התייחסו אליו כמשחק. הם החליטו לפרסם איך בונים את ה-PC שלהם — קראו לזה PC Compatible — ונתנו את זה לכל מי שרצה. אבל היה צריך גם מערכת הפעלה, ואז הגיע אליהם ילד ואמר "יש לי מערכת הפעלה". אבא של הילד היה עורך דין ידוע, ואמר "בוא נשים בלעדיות". IBM אמרה "עזוב, לא רלוונטי, נחתום וגמרנו". וכך ה-PC, כיוון שעכשיו חברות יכלו לייצר PC סטנדרטי תואם עם מערכת הפעלה אחידה, התפשט כמו אש בשדה קוצים. לאט לאט הכלי הזה נהיה יותר חזק, ישב על Local Area Networks שפותחו בזירוקס, והתחיל לתת הרבה ממה שהמיינפריים עשה — במחירים זולים. וכיוון ש-IBM פרסמו את הכל ולא השתלטו על השוק, הם הפסידו.

הדבר שהדהים אותי: היית אומר שהם התעסקו רק במיינפריימס ולא במוצרי צריכה, אבל זה לא נכון. היה להם Division ענק של מכונות כתיבה — מכונות הכתיבה עם הגולה. היה להם B2C חזק ומדהים, ואיכשהו מישהו לא דיבר עם מישהו, והם יצאו עם ה-PC וירו לעצמם ברגל. זירוקס עשו משהו דומה: הם פיתחו מחשב שהמציא את החלונות, WYSIWYG, תפריטים, עכבר, Local Area Network, Laser Printer — כל מה שאתם רואים היום במחשב המודרני פותח בזירוקס פארק (Palo Alto Research Center). הם קראו לו Star, וזירוקס אמרה "זה לא מעניין אותנו" — למה, אני עד היום לא מבין. סטיב ג'ובס כן התעניין, יצא עם ליסה ב-1985 ומיד אחרי זה עם ה-Macintosh, המחשב הראשון שמימש את הרעיונות שפותחו בזירוקס פארק. The rest is history.

שיעורי בית. למה אני נותן לכם שיעורי בית? למעלה מעשרים איש הגישו בפעם הקודמת, וכמה אנשים אמרו שהם סבלו קשות אבל זה עזר להם. אז גם הפעם תסבלו קשות. שיעורי הבית מורכבים משתי משימות. הראשונה קשורה לשמן זית. תמצאו לפחות ארבעה jobs to be done שונים שבהם שמן זית יכול לשמש — הקשרים שונים, אמוציות שונות. תבחרו שניים שהם חדשניים ומעניינים אתכם ותכתבו some copy for ads. תחשבו איך זה משפיע על המודל העסקי: איפה תמכרו את זה, באיזה מחיר, איזו אריזה. בכוונה אני נותן את המוצר הכי פשוט שקיים — חמשת אלפים שנה על כדור הארץ. הרומאים אפילו התרחצו בשמן זית. תשימו אותו במיצוב חדש. מותר להשתמש באינטרנט כי זה משעשע — אני רק רוצה שתראו את הגיוון העצום ואת האפקט שיהיה לזה כשתתחילו לחשוב למי אני מוכר, למה הוא יקנה.

הפרויקט השני — אותו דבר על המוצר שלכם. הגדירו שלושה jobs to be done שונים, עשו את הניתוח לפי functional, contextual, emotional, וכתבו קופי לכל מיצוב. תחשבו על זה מנקודת המבט של המשתמש: אם הוא הולך להשתמש במוצר שלי לצורך הזה, מה עוד הוא צריך כדי שיהיה מבסוט? נשלח לכם את זה במייל, ובעוד שבוע וחצי, ביום שני, נשמח לקבל את שיעורי הבית. תודה רבה לכם — הפעם עמדנו בלוחות הזמנים.
english_summary:
This lecture explores three interconnected frameworks — Jobs to Be Done, Positioning, and Market Segmentation — with a strong emphasis on how emotional and personal motivations drive purchasing decisions, even in B2B contexts. The central argument is that behind every business transaction stands a human being with personal interests, fears, and incentives that may not align with their company's objectives. IBM's classic FUD (Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt) strategy illustrates this perfectly: by appealing to a CIO's fear of being blamed for a system failure, IBM made itself the safe choice regardless of technical merit. Conversely, selling a labour-saving product to the very manager whose role depends on overseeing the workers it would replace is a recipe for failure, as the lecturer vividly demonstrates with a story from his time at ZoomInfo.

A recurring and powerful insight is that customers rarely want products — they want jobs done. The lecturer advocates selling outcomes rather than tools: instead of offering software that requires learning, implementation, and risk, offer the result itself as a managed service. He shares a compelling case of a founder who struggled for years to sell her product to just three clients, then pivoted to selling the output alone and saw enthusiastic demand at higher effective revenue. This principle extends to IBM's historic transformation under Lou Gerstner, who — after simply listening to customers — converted IBM from a hardware company into a professional managed-services firm, generating billions by solving what truly kept clients up at night.

The lecture also examines market segmentation through practical examples like airline pricing, where context (business versus leisure travel) determines willingness to pay and purchasing behaviour, and a portable water-heating device repositioned for jungle travellers with accessories like spare batteries and a stylish carrier. These cases reinforce that once you identify the job and context, the product design, packaging, pricing, and sales channel follow naturally.

Historical cautionary tales round out the session: IBM's failure to control the PC ecosystem it created, and Xerox's abandonment of groundbreaking innovations developed at PARC, both underscore what happens when companies lose sight of market positioning and customer needs. The lecture closes with a homework assignment asking students to apply Jobs to Be Done analysis first to a simple, ancient product — olive oil — and then to their own ventures, reinforcing that even the most familiar offering can be radically repositioned when viewed through the lens of context, emotion, and the specific job the customer needs accomplished.

ההרצאה עוסקת בתפיסת ה-Jobs to Be Done, מיצוב מוצרים וסגמנטציה של שוק, תוך שימת דגש על כך שגם בעולם ה-B2B תמיד עומד בן אדם מאחורי ההחלטה — עם רגשות, אינטרסים אישיים ושיקולים שאינם בהכרח זהים לאלה של החברה. הדוגמה המרכזית היא שיטת ה-FUD (Fear, Uncertainty and Doubt) של IBM, שבה פנו למקבל ההחלטות האישי ואמרו לו: אם המחשב ייפול, אתה תישא באחריות — ולכן עדיף לקנות IBM ולכסות את עצמך. העיקרון חוזר בדוגמאות נוספות: כשמוכרים מוצר שמחליף עובדים, חייבים לזכור שהמנהל של אותם עובדים לא ירצה לבטל את תפקידו עצמו, ולכן צריך לפנות לגורם הנכון בארגון — למשל ל-CEO ולא למנהל הביניים.

תובנה מרכזית נוספת היא שלקוחות לא רוצים מוצרים אלא תוצאות. חברות מעדיפות לשלם עבור שירות מוגמר על פני רכישת מערכת שדורשת למידה והטמעה. הסיכון נתפס כנמוך יותר, התהליך הרכשי פשוט יותר, וההחלטה קלה יותר. יזמית שניסתה למכור מערכת טכנולוגית במשך שנים ונתקעה עם שלושה לקוחות, גילתה שכשהתחילה למכור את התוצרת כפרויקט — הלקוחות שילמו בהתלהבות. הלקח: לפעמים עדיף למכור את ה-job to be done ישירות במקום את הכלי שמבצע אותו.

ההרצאה מדגימה סגמנטציה חכמה דרך חברות תעופה שמזהות אנשי עסקים לפי מועד ההזמנה וימי הטיסה, וגובות מהם מחיר גבוה יותר כי החברה משלמת ולא הנוסע עצמו. תוכניות המיילים ומחלקת העסקים מוסיפות ממד רגשי של סטטוס ונאמנות. אותו עיקרון חל גם על מוצרי יוקרה כמו שעונים ותיקי ברקין — שם הערך הוא חברתי ורגשי, לא פונקציונלי.

סיפור אישי ממחיש את החשיבות של שאילת השאלה הנכונה: בחברת ראש מערכות חושבות, לקוח הסביר שהבעיה הדחופה שלו אינה מערכת אבחון אלא מעקב אחר חלקי חילוף בשווי מאה מיליון דולר הפזורים ברכבי הטכנאים. ב-ZoomInfo, המעבר משוק ה-Head Hunters לשוק אנשי המכירות חייב שינוי מהותי במוצר, כי ה-jobs to be done שונים לחלוטין: ה-Head Hunter מחפש מחט בערימת שחת, ואיש המכירות רוצה את כל הערימה עם פרטי התקשרות מדויקים.

הנקודה המסכמת: תמיד יש לבחון את המצב מנקודת המבט של הלקוח — על מה הוא מאבד שינה, מה באמת כואב לו — ולבנות את המוצר, המיצוב והמודל העסקי סביב התשובה הזו.
